content: The naming has been adjusted. The PR looks fine to me now.
What's the hold up here? The changes requested by @Chris Henson?
Unless I'm missing something, all of the objections about duplicating Mathlib definitions, which were not just from me but several other people, still apply to this PR.

As I said, Mathlib definitions are still under development (WIP); we are happy to use them if they are complete and ready. In the middle of their progress, we should get ahead and move on. It's been a few months already.

If I remember correctly the online meeting discussion, the idea is to go forward with this and @Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai was willing to act as bridge to future mathlib modifications/discussions. Graph data structures for algorithms will take some plumbing (encodings or instances) to be convenient, but having a repository of what people consider 'easy to use' for this purpose seems useful.

Sidenote: I'm also applying very similar reasoning to the situation found in Turing Machines, where there's disagreement on what's convenient for different purposes and what basis definitions should look like.

I don't think there is any ease-of-use difference between mathlib's simplegraph and this proposal. For example I don't think labelling edges as a prop (V -> V -> Prop) is in any way a hindrance to getting the neighbouring edge set (V -> Set V). I'd still check with @Bhavik Mehta as I proposed in the meeting.
@Bhavik Mehta any opinions on this?

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I don't think there is any ease-of-use difference between mathlib's simplegraph and this proposal. For example I don't think labelling edges as a prop (V -> V -> Prop) is in any way a hindrance to getting the neighbouring edge set (V -> Set V). I'd still check with Bhavik Mehta as I proposed in the meeting.

That's not the point. The point was that Mathlib's definition of graphs remains fragmented and under development. In particular, it does not define other types of graphs in a unified way (simple/nonsimple and undirected/directed). We would like to move forward with a consistent, unified definition of graphs, and we are also happy to reuse the Mathlib version once it is ready.

In particular, it does not define other types of graphs in a unified way

I don't think adding another definition helps with that. But I am not expressing any strong opinions here, since it is better to have the opinions of those working on mathlib graph theory actively at the moment.
@Chris Henson, do you have any more comments/objection regarding the PR? Is there anything I can help you?
If there is no further objection, I would like to proceed with the PR.
I think Chris has already expressed an objection.
Yes, but I meant: does he still object despite the follow-up discussion thus far (from July 7 onwards)? Do you also strongly object?

To be clear: yes, I still have the exact same objections, because it seems that nothing has changed with regards to duplicating definitions from Mathlib. In #CSLib > New graph definitions (I think the beginning of the thread was more productive than later on...) it seemed like there was a lot of agreement on this point from @Bhavik Mehta, @Jun Kwon, and others who are familiar with this part of the library, and several discussions about things you can do that do not involve duplicating definitions. I feel just as strongly as I did then that if there is going to be any point to us having a Mathlib dependency that we work within and improve the existing framework. None of this conversation appears to have been followed up on since, so my objection remains.

Sure, @Bhavik Mehta @Jun Kwon, can you give us an estimate of when the graph definitions will be ready to use? I am talking about directed/undirected simple/nonsimple graphs. Currently, it seems undirected non-simple graphs are the ones we are happy with.

If I understand correctly here from re-re-reading the threads (:melting_face:), the point is that in mathlib some cases are missing and there's fragmentation. Is this impression correct? I understood this PR as a way to give the graph algorithm people a simple coherent layer to work on, while we wait for the mathlib discussion to settle. We would then try to upstream as much as possible and switch to the new mathlib API. The corpus we would build on graph algorithms might potentially offer some useful input as to what this new API should support.

Which of the following is the objection/suggestion as alternative?

  1. Wait for the new mathlib API to come out.
  2. Sacrifice homogeneity and introduce new graph definitions only for missing cases, and write thin APIs over existing mathlib defs for the covered cases?
  3. Something else?

The thread got a bit long, so I was left curious about this: Is there a concrete, working suggestion as to how to do 2 or something similar?

The current mathlib API is not a blocker for graph algorithms.

Edit: the new API can definitely help in many cases, but a large number of algorithms can be easily phrased in the existing setup, and adapted later.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

If I understand correctly here from re-re-reading the threads (:melting_face:), the point is that in mathlib some cases are missing and there's fragmentation. Is this impression correct? I understood this PR as a way to give the graph algorithm people a simple coherent layer to work on, while we wait for the mathlib discussion to settle. We would then try to upstream as much as possible and switch to the new mathlib API. The corpus we would build on graph algorithms might potentially offer some useful input as to what this new API should support.

Which of the following is the objection/suggestion as alternative?

  1. Wait for the new mathlib API to come out.
  2. Sacrifice homogeneity and introduce new graph definitions only for missing cases, and write thin APIs over existing mathlib defs for the covered cases?
  3. Something else?

The thread got a bit long, so I was left curious about this: Is there a concrete, working suggestion as to how to do 2 or something similar?

I would support 3 (which is in the current PR -- all set-based definitions (no relation)). Option 2 would be to use a mixture of relational and set-based definitions, as in Mathlib's simple multi-graph. (Their rationale was to avoid using Sym2 to define undirected graphs. I don't mind using Sym2 as an edge definition in undirected graphs.) However, for directed graphs, there is no Sym2 problem, and set-based definitions for both vertices and edges are more natural. I just want to have coherent, consistent definitions across all types. That's why I prefer the version in the current PR.

(There is another point -- which we may diverge from Mathlib once we talk about computation. For example, we may use typeclasses to synthesize an algorithm from the graph definition. However, this is not yet related to the PR; future work could extend it. )

all set-based definitions (no relation))

This point keeps coming up. I don't understand why you believe one is meaningfully different from the other. Mathlib has enough API to trivially switch between these two representations (after all a mathlib set is just a predicate/relation) and the difference is so thin, I don't think it merits building a separate graph API. This is essentially what was mentioned in the other thread as well.

Let me rephrase this question. Is there a concrete algorithm that you feel you can write in your representation of undirected simple graphs, that you believe is substantially harder to write with SimpleGraph in Mathlib (or with some structure extending SimpleGraph with verts : Set V). Can you show your code for this algorithm, so that someone here can adapt it to SimpleGraph (I don't have much time, I might end up asking codex to do it).

I really don't want to add noise to the discussion; you guys have the depth that I don't and won't have, but from my perspective as a software engineer in robotics who would use cslib to verify his software, I would appreciate definitions closer to those in CLRS. Ideally, these definitions should live in CSLIB. I am not sure about the long-term implications or consequences (again, I don't have the skills), but if I wanted to show that my graph works today, I would need accessible definitions rather than going to mathlib.
In light of the lack of replies from the Mathlib folks, should we proceed with it?
I haven't received a proper response to my objection

Nadim Farhat said:

I would need accessible definitions rather than going to mathlib.

For library-level formalisation, integration with the library ecosystem and generality of definitions matters more. Case in point: probability theory being in measure theoretic generality. In any case I don't see how the current mathlib set up of SimpleGraph is inaccessible. As for (multi) Graphs, yes there is missing API. But in that case adding the API to Mathlib as PRs is the ideal way to avoid duplication of work.

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

lack of replies from the Mathlib folks

Hey, I'm not sure what response you're looking for. Yeah graph theory is lacking in mathlib, and the review queue is very slow. But creating a parallel graph theory library seems like a bad idea all around.

Adding API for Graph and Digraph (e.g. walks) in a ToMathlib folder sounds like a better idea, and at some point (I think the 1st/2nd online meeting) the idea of cslib being early adopters of GraphLike was brought up which might be even better.
Thanks for the comments. I'll try GraphLike interface.
